title: Man charged with attack on Australian MP as suspect's father says she is family friend
description: Man charged with attack on Australia MP to face courtImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The community in Wangaratta remains in shock aft
body: Man charged with attack on Australia MP to face courtImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The community in Wangaratta remains in shock after the alleged attackByKaty WatsonAustralia correspondentReporting fromWangaratta, north-east Victoria and Phelan ChatterjeeA 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in the state of Victoria on Monday.The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official.Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime". Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs."Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement."All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can".Police say they will allege the incident was targeted.Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Helen Haines sits as an independent MP for the electoral division of Indi in Australia's state of VictoriaShe was airlifted there after bystanders rushed to help.A local barber who was there says he pulled the suspect out of his car."I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I was just a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish way," said Ricky Jefferies.Others who helped "didn't even check for danger", he added. "The car was still on and they sat in front of a rolling car, that's not an exaggeration."In their statement, Victoria Police say a highway patrol unit was nearby at the time of the incident and "on scene" within eight seconds of the call coming through.As they announced the charges against the 43-year-old, they said they had searched a property in Tarrawingee, around 12km (7.5 miles) from Wangaratta."At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter," they said, adding officers would maintain a presence in Wangaratta.Haines won the seat of Indi as an independent in 2019, and has since become a prominent member of the crossbench, building rapport across Australia's increasingly divided political spectrum.The community, and country, remain in shock.At a vigil on Tuesday, locals queued patiently in the aisle of the Holy Trinity Cathedral, waiting for their turn to light a candle. Priests hugged some of those who came to pay their respects.Wangaratta's main street, where Haines's office is located, had reopened to traffic. Cars slowly filed past the growing number of bouquets being left for her on the pavement.One card read: "May you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world."

schema.headline: Man charged with attack on Australian MP as suspect's father says she is family friend

title: Schools should recognise antisemitism as distinct form of harm, review says
description: Schools and colleges in England will be required to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it followin
body: Schools and colleges in England will be required to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it following a major review, the BBC understands.It means anti-Jewish hatred would be treated as a specific safeguarding risk rather than being dealt with through existing measures to stop racism and bullying.The government-commissioned review into antisemitism in education is also expected to recommend dedicated training for teachers, more consistent recording and reporting of incidents, and better education about antisemitism and modern-day Jewish life.The BBC understands it will also call for stronger guidance on political impartiality for teachers. The review, led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell, is due to be presented to Parliament on Wednesday. The government is expected to accept all 27 recommendations.It was launched amid growing concern about antisemitism in the UK, following a series of high-profile incidents including the attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester in October 2025, in which two men were killed.Separate reviews were also commissioned into antisemitism in healthcare and into public order and hate crime laws.The BBC revealed in August that the Bell review had found Jewish schoolchildren were experiencing regular harassment and abuse.It also found that headteachers of some Jewish schools were spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than educational matters.Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security advice and support to the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools.It found in the first half of 2026 that antisemitism in schools had reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year. It jumped by 59%, from 112 reported incidents in the first half of 2025 to 178 recorded over the same period in 2026.The review is also expected to recommend that the government sets up a type of hotline where school leaders can access immediate advice on tackling antisemitism.Bell told the BBC: "This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries."Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism.Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role."When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said. "We think about it a lot."Staff and pupils told the BBC they have become so used to these measures that they barely notice them anymore.Lock-in - or "in-vacuation" - drills for dealing with intruders have become second nature, even to the youngest pupils."It's a bit scary sometimes, but you know you're safe," said Livi, a Year 6 pupil."It's sad that we can't be equal to everyone else, but people don't like us just because of the way we are," added her classmate, Sadie.A group of a dozen older pupils who spoke to the BBC said that while they feel safe inside school, hearing about antisemitic attacks in the UK, including reports of pupils at other Jewish schools being harassed on their commute and at sports fixtures, has left them feeling targeted.Some said that they were reluctant to wear skullcaps or necklaces featuring the Star of David – a Jewish symbol – outside school."Other religions get to be out and wear their necklaces and be proud - I don't get why Jewish people can't do it as much," said Year 9 pupil Ilan.In response to the recommendations, the government is also expected to encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory.The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities.However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial.The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism".In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability."He added: "We have advocated these measures be accompanied by other steps including improving education about Jewish life and ensuring schools maintain their duties in relation to political impartiality."Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations.The Department for Education has declined to comment before the review is published.

schema.headline: Schools should recognise antisemitism as distinct form of harm, review says

title: Zelensky says US intelligence sharing 'works now' after talks with Trump envoy in Oslo
description: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said US intelligence sharing on deadly Russian missile attacks "works now" after talks with President Donal
body: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said US intelligence sharing on deadly Russian missile attacks "works now" after talks with President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff.The meeting in Oslo came after accusations by Kyiv that Washington was withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks, said "genuine progress" was made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details and warned that patience would be needed.Zelensky and his European allies said it was now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo when Witkoff arrives in St Petersburg on Wednesday.Witkoff was not present at the joint press conference after Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key envoy, took part in the meeting via video link.A US official later described the talks as "very productive and constructive", saying there was a "strong alignment at the working level" among the US, Ukraine and Europe on "the next steps".The official confirmed that Witkoff is due to meet President Vladimir Putin in Russia tomorrow to discuss the proposals and that Kushner will again participate virtually.Putin is yet to publicly comment on the latest developments, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov earlier said the Kremlin would listen to what Wiktoff would offer, while ruling out "any political concessions".Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.Speaking after Zelensky's news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal". He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war".Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.Russian drone attacks continued on Tuesday. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now"."Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," the Ukrainian president said.He said he also hoped for a good result on SpaceX's Starlink satellite access as well, after Ukraine's military had reported in recent days speed restrictions on the US platform used by Kyiv to carry out drone strikes against Russia.Before the Oslo talks, Zelensky said he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and Starlink.Last week, a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into speed restrictions to the Starlink network in Ukraine. And Zelensky also restated that Ukraine was "ready for negotiations" to end the war. "Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said.The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine were also discussed in Oslo, as well as energy ceasefire proposals.Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who also took part in the talks, stressed that Europe "needs to be at the table" during any discussions about how to end the Russia-Ukraine war.Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved.Rubio, who is currently on a visit to India, admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine - but he stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.European leaders meanwhile have expressed concern about recent US statements from the US towards Russia.On Monday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly"."It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy"."We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said.

schema.headline: Zelensky says US intelligence sharing 'works now' after talks with Trump envoy in Oslo

title: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra channels to close
description: The BBC is to close its BBC Three and BBC Scotland television channels in the spring, as the corporation continues to make £500m of savings over two y
body: The BBC is to close its BBC Three and BBC Scotland television channels in the spring, as the corporation continues to make £500m of savings over two years.Both services will become online-only, meaning they will continue to produce and host some content on iPlayer, without the need to fill a terrestrial TV schedule.The BBC has also announced the closure of Radio 4 Extra, which largely airs speech programmes from the BBC's archive, including comedy, drama and documentaries.BBC director-general Matt Brittin said: "We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. We all know that means tough choices."Katie Razzall: Closures make business sense, but more savings are neededDiscussing the closure of linear broadcast services, Brittin said: "Much of the great content they currently carry will still be found where audiences already enjoy them on iPlayer and Sounds. "While this follows media speculation, I recognise the confirmation of this news will be hard for audiences and colleagues."Outlining the plans, the corporation confirmed:BBC Scotland will remain a channel on iPlayer, with some content also broadcast on BBC One and BBC Two in ScotlandBBC Three commissions, supported by increased investment in content for younger audiences, will be available on BBC iPlayer and on other platforms including YouTubeSome programmes that air on Radio 4 Extra will be available on BBC Sounds - while its religious programme The Daily Service will be on BBC Sounds and local radioBBC Three, which is aimed at young audiences and launched hits such as Fleabag, Normal People and Gavin & Stacey, previously moved online in 2016, but was reinstated as a TV channel in 2022. BBC Scotland launched as a channel in 2019, broadcasting a variety of Scottish programming including news, sport, documentaries and entertainment.However, some of the shows that air on the two networks, such as Two Doors Down on BBC Scotland and Sort Your Life Out on BBC Three, are repeats of episodes originally broadcast on other more mainstream BBC channels.Both networks currently only broadcast TV programming in the evenings, although BBC Scotland simulcasts BBC Radio Scotland during the rest of the day.The BBC said that the network's nightly programme Reporting Scotland: News at Seven will not move to BBC iPlayer and will cease when the linear channel closes. Audiences will continue to be served by BBC Scotland's wider news offering, including Reporting Scotland, The Sunday Show, Radio Scotland Breakfast, Debate Night and Scotcast, the corporation said.  While Radio 4 Extra does air some original programming, its schedule is predominantly made up of archive content, much of which is available on BBC Sounds.Sir Peter Bazalgette, former chairman of ITV and production company Endemol, told BBC News: "This is a modest and pretty well-judged package."The essence of it is it protects the spending on content, it really cuts money in the distribution of programmes, and it really had to happen because the BBC has lost 30% of its revenue in 10 years."But entertainment trade union Equity said Tuesday's announcement "does not signal a thriving BBC, and we are concerned about the UK's preeminent public service broadcaster's ability to meet its duties to the fullest".Affected staff were told about the changes on Tuesday, although the proposed closure of BBC Scotland and BBC Three had been reported by some media outlets in recent weeks.The BBC is aiming to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save £500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".Around 550 job closures have already been announced in news, while more than 30 job cuts have so far been announced for BBC Sport.The newly appointed director of BBC News, Rachel Jupp, announced on Tuesday that a further £5.5m of savings were being proposed, which would represent the closure of around 100 roles. Meanwhile, several high-profile BBC TV series have been cancelled altogether in recent weeks. RuPaul's Drag Race UK, Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live at the Apollo, Football Focus, Ski Sunday and Radio 4’s The World Tonight and You & Yours are among the programmes the BBC has dropped so far.

schema.headline: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra channels to close

title: Google says cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites resolved
description: Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts.The company, on
body: Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts.The company, one of a few large cloud computing firms whose infrastructure and services underpin many online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its London data centre complex "europe-west2" early on Tuesday.Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC were among popular UK services that confirmed disruption on Tuesday morning, after thousands of reports of problems were raised by users online.The tech giant apologised to those affected and thanked customers for their patience."We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event," a Google Cloud spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday evening."Services have been restored."They added that the company would publish an analysis of the incident on its service health dashboard, external, where it provides customers with updates about the status of its cloud services globally.Cloud computing giants like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud make their services available to clients in local or regional sites around the world, which they call "regions", containing their data centres.In updates to its service dashboard on Tuesday morning, Google Cloud had said a number of its cloud services were "experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region" - its UK cloud facility in London.It later said that the issues had stemmed from a "power event" within one of its smaller data centre zones, europe-west2-b.These seemingly affected a host of popular UK platforms and services, with customers flagging issues with sites including Royal Mail, DPD and e-bike service Forest.The HM Courts and Tribunals Service also said it was aware of an issue affecting the video platform used for remote hearings.Guy Baybutt, who works for a family-run business The Veg Box Company also said he was "severely affected" by Tuesday's outage.Baybutt, who is from Preston, told the BBC the firm - which supplies fresh fruit, vegetables and other produce to customers across the UK - could not access its website to download and process customer orders amid the technical issues."We were also unable to book parcels onto DPD's system for collection, meaning orders that should have been dispatched today were at risk of being delayed," he said."To make matters worse, customers were unable to access our website to place new orders, meaning we lost valuable sales during the outage."He said that such disruptions can have "serious financial consequences" for small businesses like his own."We don't have the resources of larger companies to simply absorb lost revenue, particularly when we're dealing with fresh, perishable produce that needs to reach customers promptly," Baybutt added.

schema.headline: Google says cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites resolved

title: Mark Allen: Former world number one considering retirement after Northern Ireland Open exit
description: The 40-year-old has had a decorated career, winning 12 ranking tournaments including the 2022 UK Championship since he turned professional in 2005.Thi
body: The 40-year-old has had a decorated career, winning 12 ranking tournaments including the 2022 UK Championship since he turned professional in 2005.This year has been a challenging one for Allen, after he missed a match-winning black in the semi-final against Wu in May during the penultimate frame that would have taken him into his first World Championship final.Allen went on to lose the final frame against eventual champion Wu and has since been a notable absentee from the World Snooker Tour circuit. "The last three months have been really, really difficult and I think even just being here today is an achievement," added Allen."For me, today was not about the result or the performance, it was trying to enjoy the experience of playing one of my best mates in one of my favourite arenas, in one of my favourite tournaments."I am not going to announce [retirement] right now after a defeat, but it is something I have been contemplating for a while and something needs to change within the next six weeks before the UK Championship for me to show up."And I need to work hard on myself in the next few weeks and see what is around the corner."Allen received a warm response from his home crowd as he returned to the venue where he became back-to-back champion in 2021 and 2022.It was clear the respect that both players had for each other following the match with Allen adding he "wished Jordan well, I always do".The world number 65 said the win was "the least satisfying" he has ever had as he progressed to the last 32 to face Michael Holt. "It is overwhelming for Mark here with his family, friends and all the fans who have paid good money to see him play," said Brown."It is very difficult. I have my own battles to go through. I am in a precarious place in the rankings, and I lost my mum recently. It just puts everything into perspective.  "The general public seem to think we are just robots who just turn up to pot a few balls - it is not like that at all."Matches between Brown and Allen have always been close contests, with Tuesday's win the 39-year-old's first victory over his close friend."I really hope so," Brown replied when asked if he thought Allen would reconsider retiring."The first words I said to him today was it was great to see him back and we had a big cuddle. It is tough to see him going through that."I have no doubt he will come back. Snooker is his love, he is absolutely brilliant and he is a top bloke. I wish him all the best."

schema.headline: Mark Allen: Former world number one considering retirement after Northern Ireland Open exit

title: Sir Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr back new Beatles attraction
description: Image source, Apple Corps LtdImage caption, Artist's impression of plans for a Yellow Submarine experience at St John's BeaconByJenny ColemanNorth Wes
body: Image source, Apple Corps LtdImage caption, Artist's impression of plans for a Yellow Submarine experience at St John's BeaconByJenny ColemanNorth WestSir Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr have backed plans for a major new Beatles visitor attraction in Liverpool.The development will see The Beatles Story move from Albert Dock to the former St John's Market site, alongside a new Yellow Submarine experience at St John's Beacon.McCartney said he "can't wait" for people to be able to "step into our story", while Starr said: "Liverpool was, and still is, Music City". The attraction will feature immersive technology, original artefacts and recreated sets charting the band's rise from post-war Liverpool to international fame.Apple Corps Ltd, which manages The Beatles' creative and business interests, will take over operation of The Beatles Story in 2027 ahead of its relocation the following year.'Like Graceland or Dollywood'The attraction has been based at Albert Dock since 1990. Under the plans, it would move to the former St John's Market Hall, vacant since the market closed in 2024. At 100,000 sq ft, the new site would be more than four times the size of the current attraction, while the former Radio City tower, St John's Beacon, would house a new Yellow Submarine experience.It follows plans unveiled earlier this year for an official Beatles attraction at 3 Savile Row in London, where the band staged their final public performance during a famous rooftop concert in 1969. Fans will be able to explore seven floors of memorabilia and archive material connected to the band when it opens in 2027.Announcing the Liverpool plans, Apple Corps chief executive Tom Greene said Liverpool was getting a Beatles destination worthy of the city's musical heritage."Just like Graceland or Dollywood, it's fitting that The Beatles will have a world-class destination for fans to visit in the city where the story started," he said.Apple Corps said visitors would be taken on a journey from the band's post-war Liverpool roots through Hamburg, The Cavern, Beatlemania, Abbey Road, Shea Stadium, Savile Row and beyond.Image source, Apple Corps LtdImage caption, The attraction will tell The Beatles story using immersive technology, Apple Corps Ltd saidCommenting on the announcement Sir Paul McCartney said: "I love Liverpool. It's part of who I am, it's part of who The Beatles are."I find it incredible and humbling that people are still interested in our story and it's very exciting to me that The Beatles Story and The Beacon are being transformed in such an exciting way in the heart of Liverpool city."It couldn't have happened without Liverpool and I can't wait for people to be able to step into our story and share the experience."Tickets sold for The Beatles Story will contribute to the The Apple Corps Liverpool Trust, a charitable initiative to provide support and opportunities for emerging local artists.Ringo Starr said:  "Liverpool was, and still is, Music City."And now we are expanding The Beatles Story Experience in Liverpool - how far out. The beat goes on."I also love that proceeds from every ticket will go back to support new Liverpool artists. It is great to be part of this. Deep down I am still a scouser. I love what Apple Corps and Liverpool are doing."Image source, Apple Corps LtdImage caption, The plans will transform the former site of St Johns Market in the city centreThe project is a partnership between Apple Corps, Liverpool City Council and Liverpool City Region Combined Authority, with support from central government.Liverpool City Region Mayor Steve Rotheram said it felt right that the "definitive Beatles experience" should be located in the city where the band's story began.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "The Beatles are one of the greatest examples of what Britain can give to the world."Four young men from Liverpool changed music and popular culture forever and, more than 60 years later, their story is still a source of enormous pride for this city and for our whole country."Reflecting on what his bandmates would have made of the plans, Sir Paul McCartney said: "If you'd told us this was going to happen when we were hanging out and getting started, we'd never have believed it."Image source, Apple Corps LtdImage caption, The experience will chart The Beatles' journey from the streets of Liverpool to the world stageGet in touchTell us which stories we should cover on Merseyside

schema.headline: Sir Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr back new Beatles attraction

title: Manchester United: Michael Carrick wants clean sheets to help turn season around, starting at Como
description: "You're dead right. I can't argue with that."Michael Carrick's response was to the point.The question that prompted it in his pre-match news conferenc
body: "You're dead right. I can't argue with that."Michael Carrick's response was to the point.The question that prompted it in his pre-match news conference at a rain-lashed Giuseppe Sinigaglia stadium in Como concerned his side's failure to keep clean sheets.It was put to Carrick that it would help if United could manage some shutouts, and he was asked if he had figured out the problem.United have kept the opposition out just once in 10 games this season, against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK last month."There's definitely parts of our game we have to improve to make things easier. I am fully aware of that," said Carrick, whose side take on Como in the Champions League on Wednesday.The problem goes further than this season though.They managed six clean sheets in Carrick's 17 matches in charge last term, including two in their final three games. Prior to that they had only managed two all season, part of an overall tally of nine in 63 games under his predecessor Ruben Amorim.It is an extreme comparison given solid defence was the bedrock of Arsenal's Premier League title triumph, but the Gunners, who face Bayern Munich in Germany on Wednesday, have recorded seven clean sheets in 11 matches this season.Continuity of selection would presumably help Carrick achieve defensive stability.It has proved virtually elusive so far. Only once has Carrick been able to name the same back four, when Diogo Dalot, Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martinez and Luke Shaw started the victory against Ipswich at Old Trafford on 30 August and kept their places for the trip to Everton the following week.Carrick described his fitness update before the Como encounter as "a mixed bag".That was largely based on him saying Netherlands defender Matthijs de Ligt was "fit and ready" after 11 months on the sidelines with the back injury that required surgery in May.Yet De Ligt was on the bench at Leeds on Sunday when Martinez went off with the thigh injury that prevented him travelling to Italy, and instead Carrick turned to Noussair Mazraoui, usually a full-back, for the central slot.United's defensive resources are stretched thinner as Leny Yoro is ruled out through suspension. Shaw is still not fit and is expected to be out for "a little bit longer" than the 10 days Kobbie Mainoo is going to miss, which could mean the left-back won't return until after the November international break.To many observers, the Manchester United left-back situation was one that could have been anticipated and should have been addressed in the summer.The fact United spoke to Manchester City about Algeria international Rayan Ait-Nouri on deadline day suggests they did view it as a potential issue.After starting all 38 Premier League games last term and the first three this, Shaw has played only twice since, and the number of games missed could reach double figures before the 31-year-old returns.When Diogo Dalot lined up at left-back against Leeds, he became the fifth different player to start there for United in six games.Aside from Shaw, none of the quintet could be regarded as a natural left-back.However, after it was suggested Martinez's post-match outburst following the defeat by Atletico Madrid was partly down to 20-year-old Ayden Heaven playing at left-back, sources did point out the youngster played more often in that role than in the centre during his youth days at Arsenal.It was also suggested in the summer that United's coaching team did not believe 19-year-old Harry Amass, who was Shaw's stand-in during pre-season, was yet at the right level.Amass' single appearance so far this season, as a substitute for the final 18 minutes against Sabah, backs up that view, although Carrick has countered it."He's right in contention," Carrick said."At some point, young players need an opportunity. It's just finding the right time."Sometimes it's because there's an unfortunate thing happened to somebody else. Sometimes it's just you're doing so well we have to give you a chance."All the young players are in a similar boat. There's maybe four, five, or six of them trying to make that next step in terms of getting into the team and trying to start games, and Harry's definitely one of them."

schema.headline: Manchester United: Michael Carrick wants clean sheets to help turn season around, starting at Como

title: Failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds
description: Government failures in care settings created an environment that allowed Covid to spread like wildfire, an official inquiry has said. The sixth report
body: Government failures in care settings created an environment that allowed Covid to spread like wildfire, an official inquiry has said. The sixth report from the Covid inquiry said the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic and there was no "protective ring" put around homes as claimed by ministers at the time.There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.The 287-page report also highlighted shortages of PPE for carers and criticised the way hospital patients were discharged into care homes.It said limits on visits caused enormous harm to residents and their loved ones, though it blamed this on care homes themselves.Around 1.5 million adults were either living in care homes or receiving support in their own homes when Covid hit.Action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences, the inquiry said.Chair Baroness Hallet said a lack of testing, PPE and pre-pandemic planning combined with policy decisions early on "created an environment in which the virus could spread like wildfire"."At the critical early stages of the pandemic, not enough was done to protect those living and working in care homes," she said."The overriding focus of the UK government and devolved administrations was on protecting hospitals."Caroline, Abrahams, the charity director at Age UK, said the report was "devastating"."When Covid took off, people using social care and the staff and unpaid carers providing it were left totally exposed."She added it also demonstrated how important the overhaul of social care promised by Andy Burnham when he became prime minister was."If a national care service had already been in place... the various disasters that befell social care during the pandemic would have been lessened and some might have been avoided altogether."Meanwhile, Natalie Grayson, from the GMB union, said care workers were "left vulnerable and terribly exposed" during the pandemic which saw "care homes turned into morgues"."That cannot be allowed to happen again," she added.Nadra Ahmed, co-chair of the National Care Association, which represents care providers in England described the findings as "really upsetting", adding that the social care workforce has "never fully recovered" from the pandemic.She said we need to "start thinking about social care in a more constructive way" and the mantra that "we all had to protect the NHS" appears to have come at the cost of "some care home residents' lives".Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government would provide a "full response" to the report's recommendations "in due course".Speaking in the Commons, Cooper said she agreed that social care had been "undervalued and under-recognised" for too long."My thoughts are with all those who lost loved ones in the pandemic, and especially those who endured the immense distress and harm of visiting restrictions in care homes, which meant they could not be with loved ones even as they died," she added.

schema.headline: Failings allowed Covid 'to spread like wildfire' in care homes, inquiry finds

title: Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat
description: The outcome was celebrated almost immediately by Prime Minister Mark Carney, who said in a statement that "Albertans made a clear choice".But the move
body: The outcome was celebrated almost immediately by Prime Minister Mark Carney, who said in a statement that "Albertans made a clear choice".But the movement's leaders say their battle is long from over and that the issue could dominate Alberta politics for years to come.Jeffrey Rath, a Calgary-lawyer and one of the main spokespeople for Alberta separation, said he and others "plan to roll up our sleeves and work harder".Keith Wilson, another separatist, told supporters in Calgary that while the vote is over, "the conversation about Alberta's future in Canada and our place in Canada and our role in Canada will continue".Smith, who openly supported and campaigned for the unity vote, thanked voters for the result.The Alberta premier has been criticised for taking a "dangerous" gamble that the independence push would likely face defeat while still giving her restive base what they wanted.She lowered the petition threshold needed to get the citizen-led campaign the ballot in the first place.By making Monday's result non-binding, she got around a court decision blocking the pro-separation petition because it failed to consult indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected if the province separated.That gamble could test her leadership of the United Conservative Party, which she has led since 2022."She's lost the confidence of the (party) base," said Rath.Albertans who voted against an independence referendum told the BBC throughout the campaign that they were motivated by a desire to keep the country united, especially as Canada grapples with tariff threats from the US, its longtime ally.They also feared that an independent Alberta could be vulnerable to outside influence - or even annexation.Thomas Lukaszuk, a prominent pro-unity campaigner, told a crowd of supporters on Monday night that the early results made him proud to be Albertan.At a pro-unity results watch party in Edmonton, Lukaszuk appealled directly to separatists, saying that "some of the issues they have raised are legitimate", and that the province must do the hard work of healing the divisions laid bare by this debate."I don't want to see us doing another referendum like this ever again," Lukaszuk said.Premier Smith told CBC earlier in the week that she would not hold an independence referendum if Albertans vote against it as long as she is premier.Some of the rifts can't easily be smoothed over.The separatist sentiment has its roots in "western alienation" which is a term that has been used for decades by some in Canada's western provinces to describe a feeling of being ignored or overlooked by the federal government in central Canada.She also put nine other questions to Albertans on Monday, most that seek to give the province more autonomy from Ottawa, including on matters like immigration.The (very) preliminary results suggest that many might pass.Some who voted in favour of a second binding separation referendum have said they didn't want outright independence, but some leverage over Ottawa. Smith has said these other nine questions help give her just that.Quebec, another province with similar sovereigntist sentiments, could offer clues on where Alberta's separation movement might end up.They held two separation referendums, in 1980 and 1995, both of which were defeated by a close margin.Alberta independence supporters don't hide the fact that they gain inspiration from the majority French-speaking province.They view Quebec as having successfully used the threat of separation to gain significantly more autonomy over provincial affairs.And despite support for Quebec sovereignty being at historic lows, a newly elected provincial government has pledged to hold a third referendum on independence by 2030.Rath made a note of that as he pondered his side's defeat.The sovereigntist Parti Quebecois "has just formed the government of Quebec with 28% of the vote," he said."It's not out of the realm of possibility", he added, that Alberta separatists could do the same in the future.

schema.headline: Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat

title: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByHealth correspondentThe sixth report of the Covid inquiry is highly critical of the way the government tried to protect pe
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByHealth correspondentThe sixth report of the Covid inquiry is highly critical of the way the government tried to protect people in care settings in the UK.Around 500,000 people were living in care homes at the start of the pandemic – with another million receiving care in their own homes.The inquiry said action to protect them came too late, causing devastating consequences.There were more than 43,000 recorded deaths involving Covid in care homes between March 2020 and July 2022. Here are the key findings of the 287-page report.There was no 'protective ring'At the start of the pandemic, the then-health secretary in England, Matt Hancock, said the UK government had placed "a protective ring" around care homes.But the inquiry says this was not the case, listing a catalogue of failings.It says the care sector appeared to be "something of an afterthought".A lack of personal protective equipment (PPE) meant staff had to resort to makeshift workarounds, including bin bags, festival waterproof ponchos and painters' overalls.The report is also critical of the way hospital patients who may be infected with Covid were moved to care homes to make space for others.The decision was understandable given the need to free up beds for Covid patients. But, without sufficient testing, it was important to keep these people separate and isolate them from others in case they were infected.Official guidance in March 2020 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland did not request this. That, the report says, was a significant oversight.Long-standing weaknesses undermined responseWhen the pandemic started, high levels of staff vacancies and turnover in the social care sector meant that the workforce was "fragile and lacking resilience".This undermined the ability of the sector to respond to the pandemic, the inquiry says.For example, care homes tend to rely heavily on agency staff who work in a variety of different homes. But a desire not to have staff going into multiple homes, to reduce the risk of infection transmission, meant staff shortages got even worse.Financially, care providers struggled too, as the number of people using services dropped.And for a sector that uses zero-hours contracts, there was a lack of financial support to help care staff stay off work if there was concern they might be infected.The response also suffered because of the fragmented nature of the system, with thousands of different providers and services overseen by councils. It meant the sector was more distant from government than the NHS.The pandemic, the inquiry said, exposed and exacerbated these existing weaknesses.Visiting restrictions were too tough – and caused harmThe report is clear that precautionary steps taken to restrict visiting, as part of infection control, went too far.It acknowledges there was little choice to introduce bans on visitors at the start of the pandemic, saying that was rational.But as the pandemic progressed, so did the balance between the benefits and harms of restrictions.Visits are extremely important, allowing loved ones to help residents with everything from personal care to maintaining their mental health.By September 2020, evidence suggested visitors posed a "marginal risk" – staff were judged to be the key entry point for infections.The four UK nations then started to relax their guidance, but many care homes failed to implement this and visiting remained heavily restricted.This, says the inquiry, resulted in a significant decline in the health and wellbeing of residents.Concern over blanket do not resuscitate ordersCPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation), including chest compressions, can be life-saving if a person's heart has stopped beating.But doctors can sometimes opt not to resuscitate people - as can individuals themselves in advance - for example, if the individual is extremely frail or has a life-limiting illness. This should be done on an individual basis and the use of blanket do not resuscitate orders (DNACPR) is considered unlawful.The inquiry says it heard evidence of GPs imposing blanket DNACPRs on care home residents.And it pointed to records showing a sharp increase in orders being put in place – they jumped from 16,800 to 26,500 in the first nine months of the pandemic.This concern mirrors an earlier Care Quality Commission investigation which found evidence of unacceptable and inappropriate DNACPRs being put in place.The 'deep distress' of care staffThe impact on staff working in care homes was huge, affecting their mental health and wellbeing, the inquiry said.Some moved into the care homes where they worked, in an attempt to protect residents from infection. One care home owner in Wales described how 39 staff moved in for a fortnight at the start of the pandemic.Seeing so many residents die placed an enormous strain on workers, who often had to provide end-of-life care to multiple people at the same time.One care home, for example, lost half of its residents over the course of three weeks.Staff told the inquiry of the deep distress they suffered. "Staff were sitting on video calls with families, saying their last goodbye to loved ones. That was horrendous… staff were crying with the residents, because it was just so emotional for them," one said.

schema.headline: Covid failings in care homes: What the inquiry says

title: UK government to make Jackdaw gas field announcement
description: Jackdaw, about 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen, is a gas field which its operators say could be connected to the UK network within months.Roseban
body: Jackdaw, about 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen, is a gas field which its operators say could be connected to the UK network within months.Rosebank, about 80 miles (128.7km) north-west of Shetland, is Britain's largest untapped oil field, which would also produce some gas.The controversial fields have been the subject of years of debates, legal wrangling and public consultations, with arguments from both industry bodies and environmentalists being weighed up by the UK government.Licences for the fields were granted by the Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023, which sparked legal challenges from environmental groups.The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.Environmentalists insist more drilling would be unconscionable, and hamper efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect people across the globe.They also claim starting production would not protect energy security and transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs.Industry bodies argue starting production at Rosebank and Jackdaw will provide jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply.

schema.headline: UK government to make Jackdaw gas field announcement

title: Second Labour MP suspended over Covid loan repayments
description: A second Labour MP, Perran Moon, has been suspended over Covid loan repayments, after voluntarily referring himself for investigation.Moon, the MP for
body: A second Labour MP, Perran Moon, has been suspended over Covid loan repayments, after voluntarily referring himself for investigation.Moon, the MP for Camborne and Redruth, is listed on Companies House as the co-director of a training company called Autoswot, external, which last filed accounts in June 2021.Government Bounce Back Loans of up to £50,000 were made available to support small businesses during the pandemic, but a government report found the scheme was vulnerable to fraud and error.In August, Labour MP Bayo Alaba was suspended after queries about a Covid-era loan, and a third MP, James McMurdock, quit Reform in 2025 after questions about eligibility for loans he received.Bounce back loans worth a total of £46bn were issued when the scheme was launched in May 2020, making it the biggest of the government's pandemic-era loan schemes.Each one had a 100% government guarantee, meaning taxpayers' cash was used to pay back banks if the companies failed, but the Covid counter-fraud commissioner later found total fraud and error estimated at up to £2.8bn to the public purse.Autoswot had been set up in June 2019, a year before the loans became available, and at that time had forecast revenues of more than £200,000.Moon stressed he had applied for the maximum loan of £50,000 within the rules, regularly seeking professional advice about its obligations, and would provide documents to the Labour Party investigation into the matter. He said the loan was used to pay for "staffing and other essential business costs" during the pandemic and partial repayments were made until the company ceased trading in late 2022.The BBC understands that Moon was repeatedly assured in writing by Companies House that no accounts needed to be filed after the company applied to be struck off, but that guidance was incorrect.Moon, who was first elected in the 2024 Labour landslide following a career in communications and marketing, said the business folded due to unforeseen external market pressures and "despite the best efforts of staff".He said: "In order for these matters to be looked into, I have voluntarily referred myself to the Labour Party's investigations process and will cooperate fully with this process."The loan application was made in good faith, and the information provided, including the company's turnover forecast, was accurate and properly based."I will continue to work hard every day representing my constituents while this party process is ongoing."A Labour Party spokesperson confirmed Moon had referred himself for investigation."The Labour Party expects the highest standards from our elected representatives and we have robust processes in place to ensure those high standards are upheld," they said."We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing."This is the second investigation the Labour Party has launched into the loans, with Alaba, the MP for Southend East and Rochford, also referring himself for investigation over loans made to a real estate company, Alaba Properties.At the time, Alaba said: "There has been no attempt to avoid my financial obligations, and I am wholeheartedly committed to ensuring that the liability is met in full."McMurdock, who now sits as an independent, was the first MP to be questioned over bounce back loans given to two fitness companies worth £70,000.In 2025 McMurdock said all his business dealings had been compliant with the rules, adding that after taking "specialist legal advice" he had decided "to continue my parliamentary career as an independent MP".

schema.headline: Second Labour MP suspended over Covid loan repayments

title: Woman says she 'couldn't speak or breathe' during alleged rape by Russell Brand
description: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who says Russell Brand raped her at his home in London told police she "couldn't speak or breath
body: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who says Russell Brand raped her at his home in London told police she "couldn't speak or breathe" during the alleged attack, a jury has heard.The 51-year-old entertainer is accused of raping the woman in 2009 after meeting her at London's Hammersmith Apollo, where he had been performing as a stand-up comedian.Brand faces seven charges in the trial in total - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges.In video evidence of her speaking to a police officer, the woman said she performed a sex act on Brand at the London theatre after being invited for drinks following the show.She said she gave him her phone number, explaining she was "a massive Russell Brand fan" and a "massive comedy fan" at the time.After that night, she said Brand messaged her and she went to his house in Hampstead knowing they would have sex.But she said a consensual encounter became rape when Brand started having anal sex with her and ignored her pleas for him to stop.She said when she arrived at his home, Brand told her she needed to have a shower "because my hair smelled funny". He then asked her to brush her teeth."I was trying to make a joke of what he was making me do", she said. "All of those things made me feel, 'I don't like this'."The woman said a short while after getting on his bed, she was turned over. It was then she said she was allegedly raped.She told police: "From the very moment it happened, I felt I had willingly gone there and from what his reputation was, what did I expect?"She said Brand "hurt me and harmed me, and when I asked him to stop, he didn't". She added: "The horror in anyone that I told was not enough to make me believe I didn't deserve it."The woman said she told friends and family afterwards, and went through sexual health tests - believing that she had contracted a disease from Brand.Earlier on Tuesday, another woman who claims Brand sexually assaulted her described the alleged attack as "frenzied" and "violent".That complainant alleges Brand assaulted her at the Choice FM radio studios in central London in the mid-2000s.She said she came out of a small room in the building to find Brand outside."He said 'aye aye'," she told the jury. "He grabbed me by my face, started to kiss me, and when he was kissing me he started pushing me - his body against me."The woman continued: "He was kissing me, it was very frenzied. There was no time for me to even understand what was going on."He was running his hands over my body and I had my back against the wall at that point."From behind a blue screen, the woman described the kiss as "sloppy" and "very, very rough", when asked by the prosecution barrister about the alleged attack."His hands at the same time were all over me," she said. "He touched my bum, my breasts, his body was pressed up against me."The woman said she pushed him off and swore at him.She said there were several people with him who she claims didn't say anything about what happened after the alleged assault.The woman - now in her 50s - said she had never met Brand before and that she believed he'd been in the building because he was on Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth.She told the jury: "His whole body was pressed against me - the kisses were hard and sloppy and going down my neck. "His hands were moving so much - the reason I used the word frenzied was because it was violent. He just wasn't stopping."She said she felt "dirty" after the encounter and "never told anybody", adding: "I felt shocked and stunned, shaken."When questioned by Brand's barrister on why none of the people who may have seen what happened raised concerns, the woman said: "It was not the present-day environment.""On the day it happened - and I ask myself this question - why I didn't share it," she said. "It wasn't the culture where something happened to you and you tell people."Asked by the defence barrister why she did not go to the police, the woman said: "I would have thought about a few things. Who would have believed me?"I could lose my job and I had a mortgage to pay," she said, adding that she "buried it for so long".The woman said she came forward with the allegation after watching a documentary on television about the TV star and his alleged behaviour.Another complainant also gave evidence to the jury - again from behind a blue screen to the right side of the court.The woman, who worked with Brand on a Channel 4 project in 2009, said members of the defendant's team asked her for a massage on his behalf while they were in the same space.She said after replying no, Brand "came into the room and lay his head into my lap, into my groin area".When asked by the prosecution counsel where exactly his mouth and nose were, the woman replied "in my vaginal area".The woman who worked for channel 4 at the time - said she was "so repulsed at the situation". She described him as "bony".She said she reported the alleged incident to her line manager at the time who then reported it further up the chain.Brand stared straight ahead as the complainants gave evidence - barely changing his posture. His hands sometimes resting on his lap. His wife Laura Brand remained sitting to his right side outside the dock - seeming to listen attentively to what the women were saying from the witness box.Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.The trial continues.

schema.headline: Woman says she 'couldn't speak or breathe' during alleged rape by Russell Brand

title: King praises Strait of Hormuz peace efforts at glittering banquet
description: Figure caption, King praises Oman's 'noble efforts' to keep Strait of Hormuz openByRoyal correspondentUpdated 1 hour agoKing Charles spoke Arabic as h
body: Figure caption, King praises Oman's 'noble efforts' to keep Strait of Hormuz openByRoyal correspondentUpdated 1 hour agoKing Charles spoke Arabic as he welcomed the Sultan of Oman at a glittering state banquet in Windsor Castle.Oman is a key Middle Eastern partner of the UK, and one of the countries along the Strait of Hormuz, with the red carpet rolled out for Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said.The King's banquet speech praised the country's "noble efforts in trying to keep open one of the world's most important shipping routes".And over a dinner of pheasant and quince, he praised Oman's diplomatic mediation in the conflict with Iran to establish "where common ground might be found".Image source, ReutersImage caption, The King and Queen hosted a state banquet at Windsor Castle for the Sultan of Oman on his state visit to the UKImage source, PA MediaImage caption, The Prince and Princess of Wales were among the senior royals welcoming the Omanis to Windsor alongside the Princess RoyalThe US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran in February, killing the country's supreme leader and sparking the ongoing Iran war.The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most vital shipping lanes, has been effectively closed since then.King Charles, Queen Camilla, Prince William and Catherine and Princess Anne were among the royals on duty at Windsor for the state visit.It was the first state banquet for Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was seated next to the Omani academic and novelist, Jokha Alharthi.It was a table laden with elaborate candelabra and polished decorations, with five glasses per setting, and even the surface of the salt had an imprint of the cypher of King Charles.The hot summer meant a bumper crop of pomegranates in the Windsor Castle gardens, and the fruits were placed on the table alongside the floral decorations.The King's speech, delivered to 160 guests in English with some quotes in Arabic, expressed his approval that his son Prince William had worked on an expedition project alongside the Sultan's son."There can be few happier symbols of success than a living relationship being passed from one generation to the next," said the King.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Places were laid for 160 guests with a menu that included pheasant and Cornish crabImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Oman is a strategically important Middle East partner for the UK with the Strait of Hormuz close to the Omani coastlineImage source, ReutersImage caption, William, and his relationship with the Sultan's son Sayyid Theyazin, were referenced as a point of pride in the King's speechThe King's youngest son, Prince Harry, was not present, as he is not a working royal. But he had stolen some of the attention from the state visit, with the publication of an interview in which he said he wanted to reconcile with his family."Some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out. With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point," Prince Harry told GQ in New York.There was wine available at the banquet, but with Muslim guests of honour, the traditional banquet cocktail was replaced by a non-alcoholic spiced coffee drink.The state banquet, served in St George's Hall, offered guests:Croute of Scottish langoustine and Cornish crab with avocado, tomato consommé, and celeryPot roasted Windsor pheasant with spiced quinceStuffed cabbage and braised fondant potatoes in a Dijon mustard sauceSelection of assorted seasonal vegetablesIndividual baked Alaska with Balmoral plum and Windsor estate honey ice creamImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Guests were served salt imprinted with the King Charles III cypherEarlier on this grey autumn day, the Omani delegation had been formally welcomed by the King and Queen, before a carriage procession to Windsor Castle.State visits are a mix of pageantry and politics, with the carefully choreographed hospitality providing an opportunity for talks about business and military links.During his visit to the UK, the Sultan's delegation will be meeting UK business representatives.This visit is taking place against the sensitive background of tensions in the Middle East, with Oman facing Iran, on the other side of the strategically important Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman.The King's speech emphasised the long partnership between the UK and Oman and the importance of Oman's efforts at bridge building in a time of conflict.In response, the Sultan had said his country "seeks solutions... we believe in dialogue".On Wednesday, the Sultan will head to Downing Street for a meeting with the prime minister.

schema.headline: King praises Strait of Hormuz peace efforts at glittering banquet
